passage: The evening before the school spelling bee in Lagos, Chidi's eyes would not stop blinking. Blink, blink, sniff. He could feel each one coming, like a sneeze building behind his nose, and holding it back only made the next one bigger. "Chidi, stop that," his aunt said at dinner. He tried. His face got hot, and the blinks came faster. After dinner his cousin Omar tipped out the box of model-plane parts. They bent over the wing pieces together, gluing and arguing about the tail. An hour passed. Omar looked up. "You haven't blinked like that once since we started." Chidi hadn't noticed. He pressed the last wing into place and grinned.

qa.q: What did Chidi and Omar build after dinner?
qa.a: A model plane, gluing the wing pieces together.

qa.q: How did Chidi feel when his aunt told him to stop, and what happened?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and his face got hot, and the blinks came faster.

qa.q: What does the evening show about when Chidi's tics ease?
qa.a: They eased when he was absorbed in building the plane with Omar, so a calm, engaging activity helped more than being told to stop.

qa.q: How might Chidi's aunt respond differently if she understood the urges?
qa.a: She might stop telling him to stop, since it only made him ashamed and the blinking worse.

grounding: It shows a child with blinks and sniffs he cannot fully control, preceded by urges, rising with stress and shame and falling when he is absorbed.

passage: At the sports club, the minutes before a badminton match were the worst for Aparna. Her throat made a small clicking sound, then another, and her shoulder jerked up. The urge rose inside her like an itch she had to scratch. From the stands a parent called, "Beta, control yourself, people are looking." Aparna's face burned. Click, click, jerk. Her doubles partner, Imran, just handed her the shuttle. "Your serve." Then the rally started. Her eyes locked on the white feathers, her feet flew, and for twelve points the clicks all but disappeared. In the break Imran passed her the water bottle without a word. When the clicks came back, he carried on talking about their tactics as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: What did Imran hand Aparna before the rally?
qa.a: The shuttle, saying, 'Your serve.'

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when the parent told her to control herself?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed; her face burned and the tics got stronger.

qa.q: Which choice by Imran helped Aparna most?
qa.a: He didn't comment on the tics and just carried on with the game and the tactics talk.

qa.q: How might the parent in the stands see Aparna's tics if they understood them?
qa.a: They might see that the tics aren't a choice and that shaming her makes them worse, and stay quiet.

grounding: It shows a child with sounds and movements she cannot fully control, preceded by urges, rising with excitement and shame and falling when absorbed.

passage: On the school trip bus in Lisbon, Paulo's head jerked sideways and he made a small hooting sound. Two boys in the seat ahead turned round and stared. Then one of them jerked his own head and hooted, and they both laughed. Paulo looked out of the window. His throat felt tight. He wished he could make himself small enough to disappear. Liam, sitting beside him, didn't turn round to the boys, and he didn't whisper "ignore them." He just kept holding out the packet of crisps. "Which dinosaur are we seeing first? I vote the big one." When they got off, the teacher had a quiet word with the two boys. Liam walked beside Paulo into the museum, still talking about teeth.

qa.q: What did Liam keep holding out to Paulo?
qa.a: The packet of crisps.

qa.q: How did Paulo feel when the boys copied him, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt hurt and embarrassed; he looked out of the window with a tight throat, wishing he could disappear.

qa.q: Which choice by Liam helped Paulo most, and why?
qa.a: He simply carried on as normal, sharing crisps and chatting about dinosaurs, so Paulo felt like an ordinary friend, not a problem.

qa.q: How might the two boys see Paulo after the teacher's quiet word?
qa.a: They may realise the movements and sounds are not a joke or a choice, and stop copying him.

grounding: It shows a child with tics hurt by stares and mimicking, with a teacher stopping the mocking and a friend who carries on as normal.

passage: During silent reading, Pradeep grunted twice, loudly. Half the class spun round. Someone at the back grunted back, and giggles spread. Pradeep gripped his book so hard the page tore. His eyes stung. He had been trying to hold it in for ten whole minutes. Hafsa Ma'am closed her book. Her voice was calm but firm. "Eyes on your own pages. Pradeep has tics. They're sounds and movements his body makes that he doesn't choose, the way you don't choose a hiccup. Copying them is unkind, and it stops now." The room went quiet. Then Nivedita, next to Pradeep, slid her bookmark over so he could fix the torn page, and went on reading. At lunch Pradeep sat with her, and nobody grunted.

qa.q: What did Nivedita slide over to Pradeep?
qa.a: Her bookmark, so he could fix the torn page.

qa.q: What does Pradeep gripping his book so hard that the page tore show?
qa.a: It shows how hurt and tense he felt when the class laughed, after trying to hold in the sounds for ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Hafsa Ma'am's brief explanation change in the room?
qa.a: It made clear the tics weren't a choice and stopped the mocking, so the room went quiet.

qa.q: How does Nivedita's way of reacting differ from the back row?
qa.a: She simply helped with the torn page and carried on reading, treating Pradeep normally instead of laughing.

grounding: It shows a child with tics hurt by stares and mimicking, a teacher who briefly explains it is not a choice and stops the mocking, and a classmate who carries on normally.

passage: Dear Pallavi Di, You asked why I went straight to my room when you visited on Sunday. I want to explain properly. At school I hold my tics in all day. The shrugs, the sniffs, the little squeak. I sit on my hands and count. It's like holding a sneeze for seven hours. By the time I get home I'm so tired I can hardly speak, and then they all come out at once in my room. That's what you heard through the door. Mummy used to say, "Try harder to stop." She doesn't anymore. Last month we saw a doctor who explained what tics are and what options there are if they cause real trouble. Mummy just brings me tea now and closes the door softly. I wasn't upset with you. I was just empty. Love, your cousin-sister Minakshi

qa.q: Where do Minakshi's tics all come out at once?
qa.a: In her room, when she gets home.

qa.q: How does Minakshi feel by the time she gets home from school?
qa.a: She feels so tired she can hardly speak, after holding her tics in all day.

qa.q: What change at home helped Minakshi cope better?
qa.a: Her mother stopped telling her to try harder to stop, they saw a doctor who explained options, and now she just brings tea.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have understood Sunday before reading this letter?
qa.a: Pallavi might have thought Minakshi was upset with her, not just exhausted.

grounding: It shows a teenager who suppresses tics at school and releases them at home, tired and self-conscious, coping better when not blamed, with a doctor explaining options.

passage: "Want to know what my bus ride is like, Elizabeth? Forty minutes of holding my breath, basically. I'm Lokesh, a sixteen-year-old boy, and I've got tics. Head flicks, mostly, and a sort of cough-bark. On the bus I press my forehead against the window and try to freeze. If I let one out, the whole back row turns round. So I hold them. My neck aches by the time I get to school, and then there's six hours of the same. Then I get home and shut my door, and it's like a dam breaking. Twenty flicks in a row. I'm wiped out. My parents never tell me to stop. Dad knocks and asks, 'Dinner in ten or twenty?' That's all. Honestly, that's what helps most. At home I don't have to be on guard."

qa.q: What does Lokesh press against the bus window?
qa.a: His forehead.

qa.q: How does Lokesh feel after holding in his tics all day?
qa.a: He feels wiped out and his neck aches.

qa.q: What does Lokesh say helps most at home?
qa.a: His parents never tell him to stop; his dad just asks about dinner, so he doesn't have to be on guard.

qa.q: How might the back row on the bus see the tics if they weren't turning round?
qa.a: They might just see an ordinary passenger, and Lokesh might not feel he has to freeze for forty minutes.

grounding: It shows a teenager who suppresses tics in public and releases them at home, tired and self-conscious, who copes better when not blamed or told to stop.

passage: "People ask me what it's like sharing a hostel room with Farhan. Honestly? Normal. I'm Sumit. Farhan has tics: his arm jerks, and he says 'yup' a lot, loudly, not because he means yes. First week, I noticed. I didn't say anything. What would I say? We were arguing about whose turn it was to buy milk, and I just kept arguing. When other guys asked 'What's his deal?', I said, 'He's my roommate. He's fine.' About a month in, Farhan brought it up himself, late at night. 'You never asked about the tics.' I said, 'Didn't seem my business. Anything I can do?' He thought, then said, 'Just what you're doing.' Then he beat me at cards."

qa.q: What did Sumit and Farhan argue about in the first week?
qa.a: Whose turn it was to buy milk.

qa.q: What does Farhan saying 'You never asked about the tics' suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he noticed and appreciated that Sumit treated him normally, and felt accepted.

qa.q: Which of Sumit's choices made Farhan feel accepted?
qa.a: Sumit never commented or asked Farhan to stop, carried on normally, and only talked about the tics when Farhan raised them.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt if Sumit had asked about the tics in the first week?
qa.a: He might have felt singled out and watched, instead of just being a roommate.

grounding: It shows a wise friend who does not comment on or imitate tics, carries on normally and acknowledges them only when the person raises it.

passage: I'm Ira, and I've worked with Aparna for two years. I learned something from her in a team meeting last week. A new analyst, Kunal, joined us. During his first presentation his shoulder jerked, and he made a quick sniffing sound, again and again. A couple of people glanced at each other. One raised an eyebrow at me. Aparna didn't glance at anyone. She kept her eyes on Kunal's slides and asked, "Can you go back to the chart on sales by region?" as if nothing else was happening. The others followed her lead. Afterwards, by the coffee machine, Kunal said to her, "I have tics, by the way." She said, "Thanks for telling me. Anything you'd like from us?" He said, "No, that was perfect."

qa.q: What did Aparna ask Kunal to go back to?
qa.a: The chart on sales by region.

qa.q: What does Kunal's reply 'that was perfect' suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt accepted and relieved that the team treated him normally.

qa.q: Which of Aparna's choices set the tone for the team?
qa.a: She kept her eyes on the slides and carried on the discussion, not glancing at anyone, and the others followed.

qa.q: How might the colleague who raised an eyebrow see things after watching Aparna?
qa.a: They might realise that carrying on normally is the respectful response, not exchanging looks.

grounding: A colleague watches a wise coworker who ignores tics respectfully, carries on the conversation and acknowledges them only when the person raises it.

subtype: Worry showing as stomach aches and clinging [Actor]
passage: Every morning before the school bus, Charu said her tummy hurt. At the stop in their small town, she clung to her father's leg and cried. "What if the bus doesn't bring me back? What if you're not here?" Hemant knelt. He didn't say, "Don't be silly." He said, "Your tummy feels the worry. That's real." They made a routine: same rhyme on the walk, same wave at the neem tree. The first day, he rode the bus with her. The next week, he waved from the stop and stood right there when the bus came back. By the end of the month, Charu let go at the neem tree herself.

qa.q: Where did Charu and Hemant wave every morning?
qa.a: At the neem tree.

qa.q: Why did Charu's tummy hurt before the bus?
qa.a: She was frightened, worrying that the bus wouldn't bring her back or that her father wouldn't be there.

qa.q: What small steps helped Charu most?
qa.a: A calm, fixed routine and gradual steps: riding the bus with her first, then waving from the stop and always being there when she returned.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant had said, 'Don't be silly'?
qa.a: Charu might feel her worry wasn't believed and cling harder, since her fear would feel even more alone.

grounding: It shows a young child with tummy aches and clinging before school and many what-if questions, helped by a calm routine and gentle steps toward the bus.

subtype: Worry showing as stomach aches and clinging [Actor]
passage: At the pool in Helsinki, Valentina sat on the bench in her swimsuit, holding her stomach. "Papa, my tummy hurts. What if the water goes in my nose? What if I sink?" Sami sat down beside her. "Worry can make your tummy hurt. Let's go slowly. Today, we just watch." They watched the other children splash. The next Saturday, Valentina sat on the edge and put her toes in. "It's cold!" she squeaked. The next, she stood in the shallow end, holding Sami's hand, while the teacher showed her how to blow bubbles. In the changing room afterwards, she said, "My tummy didn't hurt today, Papa."

qa.q: What did Valentina and Sami do at the pool on the first day?
qa.a: They just watched the other children splash.

qa.q: What was Valentina worried about at the pool?
qa.a: She was worried water would go in her nose and that she would sink.

qa.q: Which approach did Sami choose, and why did it work?
qa.a: He went slowly, one small step each week, from watching to toes to standing in the shallow end, so her fear shrank.

qa.q: How might the swimming teacher see Valentina's progress?
qa.a: The teacher might see a child growing braver week by week, ready to learn bubbles once she felt safe.

grounding: It shows a young child with a tummy ache and what-if questions before swimming, and a father who uses calm, gentle steps toward the feared water.

passage: Vasudha had skipped three birthday parties this year. Each time, as soon as Mummy said, "Fine, stay home," the tightness in her chest melted. It felt wonderful. And the next invitation felt even scarier. Now it was Nazia's sleepover, and it was pouring. "What if I can't sleep? What if I cry and everyone sees?" Mummy sat on the bed. "Let's try a smaller step. Go for dinner and the film. I'll pick you up at nine." "But it's raining. What if you can't come?" "Then I'll come late, with the big umbrella. I will come." At nine, Mummy was at Nazia's door, soaked to the knees. Vasudha ran out, glowing. "We made pizza! Next time, maybe I'll stay till ten."

qa.q: What time did Mummy promise to pick Vasudha up?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel each time she was allowed to skip a party?
qa.a: She felt relief as the tightness in her chest melted, but the next invitation felt even scarier.

qa.q: What small step helped Vasudha face the sleepover?
qa.a: Going just for dinner and the film, with a firm promise of a nine o'clock pickup, even in the rain.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel about Vasudha coming, even for part of the evening?
qa.a: Nazia would likely be glad her friend came and made pizza, instead of missing her again.

grounding: It shows a child who avoids parties and sleepovers out of fear and feels relief when excused, and a smaller, supported step that is wiser than avoiding.

passage: On the morning of the science exam, Disha woke with a pounding head and begged to stay home from her Pune school. Last term she had missed two exams the same way, and each time, once she was allowed to stay home, she felt instantly better. This time her mother phoned the school counsellor, Rehana Ma'am, first. "Let her come," Rehana said. "She can write the paper in the small room next to my office, with only one other student. We'll build up to the big hall." Disha sat in the small room with her hands shaking. Rehana Ma'am smiled through the glass door, and Disha wrote the first answer, then the next. Two weeks later, for the maths paper, Disha sat in the big hall, near the door.

qa.q: Where did Disha write the science paper?
qa.a: In the small room next to the counsellor's office, with only one other student.

qa.q: Why did Disha feel better whenever she stayed home from an exam?
qa.a: Staying home took away the frightening situation, so she felt instant relief.

qa.q: What was the key choice that changed the pattern?
qa.a: Instead of letting Disha stay home again, her mother and the counsellor gave her a smaller, supported step toward the exam.

qa.q: How might Disha's mother feel watching her sit the maths paper in the big hall?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and relieved that the small steps worked instead of the avoidance growing.

grounding: It shows a child who avoids exam days and feels relief when excused, and a counsellor and parent who plan supportive small exposures instead.

passage: Thursday Lakshmi asked me "Is this right, Sir?" eleven times during one maths lesson. I counted. Her eyes filled up when I said, "You already know it is." She hardly speaks at break, just stands near the classroom door. I nearly said "Stop worrying" again. It didn't help last week. Instead, at the end of the day I sat beside her and asked quietly, "What's the scariest part of maths for you?" She whispered, "Getting it wrong and Amma being sad." I called her mother tonight. We agreed on a plan: Lakshmi gets two check-in cards a lesson; after those, she has a go on her own. At home they'll try the same. She's a kind, careful child. I want her to feel safe, not rescued every minute. - Akash

qa.q: How many times did Lakshmi ask 'Is this right, Sir?' in one lesson?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi afraid of, according to her whisper?
qa.a: She was afraid of getting it wrong and her Amma being sad.

qa.q: What plan did Akash agree on with Lakshmi's mother?
qa.a: Lakshmi gets two check-in cards a lesson and then has a go on her own, with the same idea at home.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's mother feel after Akash's call?
qa.a: She may feel concerned but reassured that the teacher noticed and is working with her on a calm plan.

grounding: A teacher notices a child seeking constant reassurance and tearful, uses gentle questions and a calm tone, and makes a plan with the family that neither dismisses nor feeds the worry.

passage: Since his father left for work in the city, eight-year-old Manoj had grown very quiet. At the village well, at the shop, at night, he asked Jaya the same thing: "Will Papa come back? What if he doesn't?" At first she said, "Of course he will, don't ask again." He asked twice as often. Then one evening, while shelling peas on the step, she asked softly, "What makes you think he won't?" Manoj's lip wobbled. "Raju's father went and never came." Jaya put the peas down. She didn't laugh or scold. She called his father on the phone that night, and his teacher the next day. Together they made a calendar on the kitchen wall with call days ticked in red and the day Papa comes home circled. Each morning Manoj ticked one box himself.

qa.q: What did Jaya and Manoj make on the kitchen wall?
qa.a: A calendar with call days ticked in red and the day Papa comes home circled.

qa.q: Why was Manoj so worried his father wouldn't come back?
qa.a: Raju's father went to work away and never came back, so Manoj feared the same.

qa.q: Which change in Jaya's approach helped?
qa.a: She stopped brushing off his question and asked gently what made him think so, then made a plan with his father and teacher.

qa.q: How might Manoj's father feel when Jaya called him?
qa.a: He might feel concerned for his son and glad to be part of the calendar plan, calling on the red days.

grounding: A parent notices a child who is quiet and constantly seeks reassurance, asks gentle questions, and makes a plan with the family and teacher.

passage: Week one. Karthik lay awake till three, running through it: what if he failed chemistry, what if the headache meant something serious, what if his friends were laughing at him in the group chat. At breakfast, when his sister Ganga asked for the salt, he snapped at her. Week four. It hadn't stopped. He'd dropped cricket practice because his mind wouldn't sit still long enough to bat. Ganga found him at midnight on the balcony, jaw tight. "It's every night, isn't it?" He nodded. Week five. Ganga walked with him to the school counsellor's room. "I'll wait outside," she said. Inside, Karthik said it out loud for the first time: "I can't stop the what-ifs." The counsellor listened, then said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's work on this together."

qa.q: What did Karthik drop because his mind wouldn't sit still?
qa.a: Cricket practice.

qa.q: What was Karthik worried about at night in week one?
qa.a: He worried he would fail chemistry, that his headache meant something serious, and that his friends were laughing at him.

qa.q: What turning point came in week five?
qa.a: With Ganga's support, Karthik went to the school counsellor and said the worries out loud for the first time.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt when Karthik snapped at her?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt at first, but later saw it was part of how tense and sleepless he was.

grounding: It shows a teenager who is tense, sleepless and irritable from constant what-ifs that last and limit his life, and who talks to a counsellor.

passage: "Ojas, you think Bhavna Bua was always this calm? Sit down. When I was sixteen, I couldn't sleep for months. Every night my head ran in circles. What if I fail? What if this cough is something bad? What if my friends secretly hate me? I stopped going to badminton. I snapped at your father, poor boy, over nothing. Everyone said, 'She's just moody. Teenagers.' But it wasn't just moodiness. It went on and on, and my world was getting smaller. My English teacher noticed I'd stopped smiling. She took me to the school counsellor. I was embarrassed. But talking to her, week after week, taught me to catch the what-ifs before they ran away with me. So if your head won't stop at night, beta, don't wait. Tell me. We'll find someone to talk to."

qa.q: What sport did Bhavna Bua stop going to?
qa.a: Badminton.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel about going to the counsellor at first?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed.

qa.q: What does Bhavna Bua advise Ojas to do if Ojas's head won't stop at night?
qa.a: Not to wait, but to tell her so they can find someone to talk to.

qa.q: How might the people who called Bhavna 'just moody' have seen her differently?
qa.a: If they had understood, they would have seen a teenager struggling with anxiety that lasted and limited her life, not simple moodiness.

grounding: An aunt recalls her own teenage years of sleeplessness and constant what-ifs that lasted and limited her life, and how talking to a counsellor helped.

passage: Kiran: can't sleep again. the trip is tomorrow Kiran: what if I have a panic on the bus Mohit: that sounds really scary. I'm here Kiran: everyone keeps saying just relax lol Mohit: I won't say that. it doesn't work Mohit: what's one small thing that would make tomorrow easier Kiran: sitting near the front? and knowing I can text you Mohit: I'll save you the front seat. text me anytime Mohit: also, you've barely slept all week. phone down, water, lights off? Kiran: ok. trying [Three weeks later] Kiran: it's still happening. not just trips now Mohit: then it's bigger than nerves. would you talk to the school counsellor? I'll walk there with you Kiran: ...ok. Monday

qa.q: Where did Kiran want to sit on the bus?
qa.a: Near the front.

qa.q: What was Kiran worried about the night before the trip?
qa.a: Kiran was worried about having a panic on the bus.

qa.q: What small step did Mohit help Kiran take?
qa.a: Mohit asked for one thing that would make tomorrow easier, saved Kiran the front seat, and also encouraged sleep.

qa.q: How does Mohit see things differently three weeks later?

passage: For weeks, Yamini had frozen at the bus stand in their kasba. The coaching classes were in the district town, an hour away, and every morning her chest went tight as the bus pulled in. Twice she walked home instead. Yusuf, her friend since primary school, didn't tell her to relax. "What's the smallest step you could manage?" "Maybe... just standing at the stand with you. Not getting on." So they stood there on Monday and Tuesday. On Wednesday she got on, and Yusuf rode one stop with her before getting off. In the evenings he dragged her on walks along the canal. "You sleep better after," he said. When the tightness still hadn't gone after two months, Yusuf said, "I think you should talk to the counsellor at the college. I'll come with you to ask."

qa.q: Where did Yusuf and Yamini walk in the evenings?
qa.a: Along the canal.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel every morning as the bus pulled in?
qa.a: She felt afraid; her chest went tight and she sometimes walked home instead.

qa.q: Which approach did Yusuf use that worked?
qa.a: He asked for the smallest step, stood with her and rode one stop, and encouraged evening walks for sleep.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see Yamini's struggle when it keeps going?
qa.a: He sees it needs more than friendship and suggests the college counsellor, offering to go with her.

grounding: It shows a friend who does not tell someone to relax, helps her take small steps, encourages sleep and movement, and suggests a professional when anxiety lasts.

passage: Supervisor's note, new trainee check-in Ira joined our Pune office three weeks ago from a small town. Her work is careful and quick. But I've noticed a few things. She often takes long breaks in the stairwell. Twice in meetings her breathing looked fast and shallow, and her hands were gripping the table. When I ask how she is, she says "All good!" too brightly. What I did next: I asked her for a quiet word in an empty meeting room. I said I wasn't worried about her work, only about her. After a long pause she said her thoughts race at night and her chest goes tight, and she's scared she won't cope here. I thanked her for telling me. I gave her the number for the company's counselling service and suggested a check-up with a doctor too. She booked both before she left. - Darshan

qa.q: Where does Ira often take long breaks?
qa.a: In the stairwell.

qa.q: What was Ira scared of, according to what she finally shared?
qa.a: She was scared she won't cope in the new place, with racing thoughts at night and a tight chest.

qa.q: Which of Darshan's choices made it easier for Ira to open up?
qa.a: Darshan spoke to her privately and made clear the concern was about her, not her work.

qa.q: How might Ira experience the quiet word differently from the usual 'How are you?'
qa.a: The private, caring question may feel safe enough to answer honestly instead of saying 'All good!'

grounding: A supervisor notices a young adult in a new city hiding racing thoughts, tight chest and fear of not coping, and supports her in sharing and seeking professional help.

passage: 14 August, hostel room, Delhi Third week of college. Everyone thinks I'm settling in fine. I post photos of the canteen and smile at orientation. Inside, my thoughts go a hundred miles an hour. What if I fail the first test? What if I've made a mistake coming this far? Last night my chest felt so tight I sat on the bathroom floor till two. I didn't tell Amma. She'll panic. But today I called Swati Di. I told her everything, even the bathroom floor. She didn't laugh. She said, "Getting help early is the strong thing to do." She stayed on the call while I filled in the campus counselling form, and she made me promise to see the campus doctor about my chest too. Appointment is Friday. I feel lighter already. - Suraj

qa.q: Where did Suraj sit till two last night?
qa.a: On the bathroom floor.

qa.q: Why did Suraj not tell Amma?
qa.a: Suraj worried that Amma would panic.

qa.q: What turning point came when Suraj called Swati Di?
qa.a: Suraj shared everything, and with Swati Di's support filled in the counselling form and promised to see the campus doctor.

qa.q: How might Swati Di feel after this call?
qa.a: She may feel worried for Suraj but glad Suraj told her and took early steps toward help.

grounding: It shows a young adult in a new city with racing thoughts, a tight chest and fear of not coping, who hides it and then shares and seeks help early.
